newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Ansett union will boost Air NZ - Matthew.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Ansett union will boost Air NZ - Matthew.

text.p: Air New Zealand's profit next year and beyond will be significantly boosted by lower costs, stronger revenues and synergies from its recent Ansett Australia marriage, chairman Bob Matthew said on Wednesday.
But Air NZ, hit by a rising New Zealand dollar and a slowing domestic economy, would see net profit in the June 1997 year fall from the NZ$225 million it made last year.
Analysts wonder how it will get an adequate return from the NZ$540 million invested for half of Ansett -- whether by equity accounted profit or better markets for Air NZ.
Matthew told Reuters in an interview that Ansett was making good progress on cutting costs, as was Air NZ.
"The dominant contribution in the foreseeable future will be Ansett enhancing its performance -- the return of its core business to profitability."
But he added: "There are not inconsiderable sums able to be achieved by the two airlines working closely together."
Efficiencies were being made in marketing and progressively in terms of sharing capacities and selling joint products.
As well, Air NZ was on the verge of making the first of probably several significant alliances with major players -- possibly one each from North America, Asia and Europe.
"There is revenue enhancement generally as Air New Zealand and separately Ansett improve their asset utilisation," Matthew said.
Ansett's profitability would improve as it moved to appropriately match airliner capacity with its market.
Air NZ had expanded its capacity by a quarter over the past two years when the market went flat and that had put pressure on yields.
"That pendulum is swinging the other way and with us planning virtually no capacity increases over a two year period we have to be optimistic that we can enhance yields or margins," Matthew said.
There had been some improvement in margins over August and September, he said. Part of the that had resulted from the recent collapse of discount airline Kiwi Air.
Although Ansett and Air NZ would be kept separate -- the other half of Ansett is owned by News Corp -- Matthew expects efficiencies from common standards, sales systems, and seamless ticketing.
Floating Ansett was an option in future.

"It could be a prospect, it's not something that is on any agenda today, but one could envisage that," said Matthew, who is also chairman of Brierley Investments Ltd. BIL has a 42.5 percent stake in Air NZ.
"These are capital intensive industries. They require a wider capital base than Air New Zealand and BIL have."
Matthew said that once alliances were formed in areas where Air NZ and Ansett were weak, there would be a gradual move away from selling just the Ansett and Air NZ brands.
"I can envisage a day when we will be selling airline systems as distinct from brands -- combinations of three or four brands," he said.

But Air NZ is likely to retain the Freedom Air brand, which was set up to compete against Kiwi Air. Matthew saw a continuing role for the budget discount airlines on short haul routes and airline companies would have to target their brands as supermarket chains currently do.
Meanwhile, he doubted Freedom was turning a profit.
Matthew warned that while Air NZ was partially insulated against the rising New Zealand currency -- for each $10 dollars of revenue lost costs shrink $6 -- New Zealand as a destination would suffer.
"There is no doubt we are vulnerable to a higher dollar. We are already quite an expensive place to visit, add another 10 percent to everything -- it is a sensitive influence."
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
